oe.title: Determining concentrations of ions in a tap water sample
points: Atomic absorption spectroscopy (AAS) for metal ions (Na^+, Mg^2+, Ca^2+, Al^3+, Fe^2+, Mn^2+, Cu^2+): each element absorbs at characteristic wavelengths. Make a calibration graph of absorbance vs concentration using standards, then read off the sample.

Colorimetry: convert the ion to a strongly coloured species (e.g. Mn^2+ → MnO_4^−, Fe^2+ with a complexing agent, Cu^2+ with NH_3 → deep blue [Cu(NH_3)_4]^2+). Use a filter of the complementary colour, a blank, standards and a calibration graph.
Complexometric (EDTA) titration for Ca^2+/Mg^2+ (hardness), with an indicator; EDTA reacts 1:1 with metal ions.

Gravimetric analysis: Cl^− precipitated as AgCl (add AgNO_3), SO_4^2− as BaSO_4 (add BaCl_2). Filter, wash, dry to constant mass, weigh. Or titrate Cl^− with AgNO_3 (volumetric). Low concentrations may need large samples.
Good practice: standard solutions in volumetric flasks, accurate pipettes, repeat/concordant results, and controls of known concentration.
equations: Ag^+(aq) + Cl^−(aq) → AgCl(s);   Ba^2+(aq) + SO_4^2−(aq) → BaSO_4(s)
diagrams: Calibration graph (absorbance vs concentration) showing an unknown read off.

oe.title: Likely pH range of human urine
points: Water itself is neutral (pH 7 at 25 °C; ~6.8 at body temperature 37 °C as K_w increases).
Acidic solutes: carboxylic acids, uric acid (weak acid, partially dissociated, N–H/O–H can donate H^+), so they lower pH.
Basic solutes: urea and creatinine contain amine/amide N with lone pairs (weak bases); creatinine accepts H^+, raising pH.
Salts: salts of weak acids (e.g. phosphate, carbonate, carboxylates) give alkaline solutions; salts of weak bases (NH_4^+) give acidic ones.
Mixtures of weak acids and their salts (e.g. H_2PO_4^−/HPO_4^2−) act as buffers, keeping pH in a range.
Overall the solution is likely slightly acidic, about pH 5–7 (actual range ~4.5–8, varying with diet and time of day), since weak acids dominate. Concentrations are low, so pH won't be extreme.
Could be checked with a pH meter (calibrated) or universal indicator paper.
equations: Weak acid: pH = ½pK_a − ½log c — e.g. 0.001 mol l^−1 acid with pK_a 4.8 gives pH = 2.4 + 1.5 = 3.9 (upper limit of acidity, before buffering)
HA + H_2O ⇌ H_3O^+ + A^−;   B + H_2O ⇌ BH^+ + OH^−
diagrams: pH scale marking where urine is likely to sit.
Structures of urea/creatinine/uric acid with acidic H and basic N lone pairs circled.
